name: Retail Banking
description: Provision of deposit-taking, lending, and payment services to individual consumers under a UK banking licence. This capability is the primary relationship owner for mass-market and mass-affluent personal customers — it holds the current account, originating savings and lending products, and acts as the distribution hub for insurance and mortgage products. It is mandated by the bank's PRA authorisation and bounded by the FCA's retail conduct regime.
mandate_source: FCA Handbook — BCOBS (Banking: Conduct of Business sourcebook)
FCA Handbook — MCOB (Mortgages and Home Finance: Conduct of Business sourcebook)
FCA Handbook — ICOBS (Insurance: Conduct of Business sourcebook)
Current Account Switch Service (CASS) rules — Pay.UK

table_stakes: Free-if-in-credit current account with debit card (Visa/Mastercard)
Instant account opening (increasingly mobile-first) — neobanks have set 5-minute KYC as baseline expectation
Real-time payments via Faster Payments and CHAPS
FSCS protection up to £85,000 prominently communicated
Online and mobile banking with push notifications
Overdraft facility (authorised and unarranged, post-FCA reform now single interest rate)
Easy-access savings account linked to current account
Open Banking / PSD2 APIs (mandatory under PSR 2017)
differentiators: Personalised financial insights and budgeting tools (Monzo, Starling lead; incumbents catching up)
Near-instant international transfers at mid-market FX rates (Revolut, Wise set expectation)
Premium current account bundles with travel insurance, breakdown cover, worldwide family cover (Lloyds Black, Barclays Blue Rewards, NatWest Reward)
Mortgage-to-savings rate differential used as retention lever by major incumbents
Branch network as trust signal for mass-market and older demographics (HSBC, Lloyds, Barclays maintain selective network)
Relationship banking for mass-affluent (Private Banking lite) — NatWest Premier, Lloyds Platinum
Credit score visibility and proactive lending pre-approval (Monzo, NatWest)
Round-up and auto-save features (Starling Goals, Monzo Pots, Chase UK round-up)
Employer salary advance integration (neobank differentiator, eroding overdraft revenue)
Cashback rewards and merchant offers (Chase UK 1% cashback as disruptive acquisition play)
disruptors: Monzo (9m+ UK accounts, 2024): default bank for under-35s, profitable in UK, expanding into lending and investments; Monzo Plus/Max premium tiers growing
Starling Bank (4m+ accounts, profitable since 2021): known for business banking but strong in retail; BaaS model via Engine platform
Revolut (10m+ UK users, 2024 UK banking licence): super-app strategy — banking, trading, crypto, insurance, travel; aggressive FX pricing pressures incumbent international transfer margin
Chase UK (Backed by JPMorgan, launched 2021): 1% cashback offer as structural loss-leader to acquire mass-affluent customers; no branch overhead; technology-first
Wise (formerly TransferWise): not a bank but holds the international payments mind-share; accounts product growing; erodes FX fee revenue
Atom Bank: digital mortgage specialist, erodes margin on fixed-rate residential mortgages
Zopa Bank: digital personal lending and savings, credit card challenger — signals that purely savings+lending propositions are viable without a current account
Kroo: social/group spending neobank, targeting younger demographics
unbundling: Savings: Chip, Plum, Zopa, Raisin UK (marketplace) attracting deposits with higher easy-access and fixed-rate interest — margin flight risk when base rate is elevated
Personal lending / BNPL: Klarna, Clearpay, Laybuy, PayPal Pay in 3 unbundling point-of-purchase credit from the bank relationship; regulation being extended to BNPL under FCA (expected 2025)
Mortgages: Habito (digital broker), Molo (digital lender), Atom Bank, Perenna (long-term fixed-rate specialist) — origination is being unbundled from the banking relationship
Insurance: Bought By Many (pet), Lemonade UK launch, Zego (gig economy) — specialist insurtechs bypassing bancassurance distribution
FX / international transfers: Wise, Revolut, OFX — near-total unbundling of international payments from the bank relationship for frequent travellers
Credit cards: New Day (Aqua, Marbles), Capital One UK, Vanquis — specialist near-prime lending operating independent of the current account relationship
Micro-investing / wealth: Moneybox, Nutmeg (now Chase), Freetrade — capturing savings and investment flows that would historically go to ISAs and current account deposits
rebundling: Monzo: current account + savings pots + investments + credit card (Monzo Flex) + premium subscription — full rebundle without branch
Revolut: banking + FX + crypto + trading + travel insurance + SIM — super-app rebundle across financial and adjacent services
Chase UK: current account + savings + investments (via Nutmeg) — JPMorgan rebundle using digital-only model
Starling: current account + marketplace of third-party financial products — open banking-native rebundle
Lloyds Group (incumbents): current account + Lloyds Bank + Halifax + Bank of Scotland + Scottish Widows (insurance/pensions) + Schroders Personal Wealth — conglomerate rebundle
switching_drivers: CASS data (Pay.UK 2023): Nationwide, Monzo, and Starling are consistent net CASS gainers; Barclays, RBS/NatWest, and Santander are net losers
Overdraft pricing transparency: FCA 2020 reform (single APR) eroded overdraft income but reduced mis-selling; price comparison now easier, accelerating rate sensitivity

Interest rates on savings: when base rate elevated (2022-2024), customers switched or split accounts to access better easy-access rates; neobanks and challenger savings platforms were primary beneficiaries
App experience and reliability: Monzo's push notification speed and spending categorisation became reference standard; incumbents with poor mobile apps lose younger customers at account opening
Ethical banking / ESG: Triodos, Starling (B-Corp), Monzo sustainability messaging attracts purpose-driven customers; incumbents face scrutiny over fossil fuel lending
Fee transparency: hidden charges and complex fee structures drive switching; neobanks' no-fee model (at entry level) is a sustained switching argument
Employer switching: many employers now pay salaries directly to Monzo/Starling, reducing friction to use neobank as primary account

current: Consumer Duty (PS22/9, effective 31 July 2023 for new products, 31 July 2024 for closed book): four outcomes — products and services, price and value, consumer understanding, consumer support. Highest conduct burden the FCA has imposed in a decade. Requires ongoing fair value assessments and clear evidence of good outcomes.
FCA Overdraft Reforms (PS19/16, effective April 2020): single interest rate, no fixed fees, no higher rate for unarranged; significantly reduced overdraft revenue for all banks

Persistent Debt rules (CONC 6.7): lenders must identify customers in persistent debt (paying more in interest/charges than principal over 18 months), prompt repayment, and after 36 months suspend credit and offer sustainable repayment

Breathing Space (Debt Respite Scheme Regulations 2020): 60-day moratorium on enforcement for customers in debt advice; mental health crisis moratorium with no time limit. Banks must halt collection and interest accrual.

Vulnerable Customer Guidance (FG21/1, July 2021): binding FCA guidance requiring banks to identify and respond to customer vulnerability across all products and channels; Consumer Duty embeds this further
Open Banking / PSD2 (PSR 2017 + FCA RTS): mandatory API access for account information and payment initiation; CMA9 must maintain premium APIs
FSCS deposit protection: £85,000 per person per authorised firm; temporary high balance protection (£1m, 6 months) for life events
Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) under PSR 2017 / EBA RTS: 3DS2 for card payments, app-based authentication for open banking
Consumer Credit Act 1974 (as amended): governs personal loans, overdrafts, credit cards — Section 75 liability, cooling-off rights, APR disclosure
incoming_2_3_years: BNPL Regulation (FCA, expected 2025-2026): Klarna, Clearpay, and other BNPL providers will be brought within Consumer Credit Act and FCA CONC; banks offering instalment credit at POS will benefit from level playing field; BNPL providers must complete affordability assessments

Retail CBDCs / Digital Pound (Bank of England, design phase 2024-2025, earliest issuance late 2020s): programmable money could disintermediate deposit accounts; bank must plan for digital pound wallet integration

Open Banking to Open Finance (FCA roadmap, Data (Use and Access) Bill 2024): extension of data portability from payments to mortgages, savings, pensions, insurance; increases switching competition and requires broader API investment

Consumer Duty closed-book deadline (31 July 2024, now passed): ongoing obligation to demonstrate fair value — expect FCA thematic reviews targeting loyalty penalties on savings and mortgage reversionary rates

FCA Consumer Credit reform (post-CCA review): FCA taking over regulation of CCA from Treasury; expected simplification of disclosure rules but stronger outcomes focus — affects personal loans, overdrafts, credit cards

Edinburgh Reforms (HM Treasury, 2022 ongoing): deregulatory package — ring-fencing threshold raised to £35bn (from £25bn); potential relaxation of ring-fence rules for smaller banks benefits mid-tier banks

PRA Strong and Simple framework: proportionate prudential regime for smaller banks (below £15bn assets); reduces regulatory overhead for challenger banks, potentially narrowing compliance cost advantage incumbents held

AI Act (EU, UK expected to follow): governance requirements on AI used in credit decisioning, fraud detection, customer communications — banks must document AI model risk and demonstrate non-discrimination
Sustainability Disclosure Requirements (SDR, FCA 2024): labelling regime for ESG products; retail banking products (green mortgages, green savings) affected; greenwashing enforcement risk

APP Fraud reimbursement (PSR, October 2024): mandatory reimbursement for authorised push payment fraud up to £85,000 within 5 days; significant operational and financial exposure for retail banks; sends and receiving PSPs share liability 50/50
enforcement_signals: FCA Dear CEO letters (2022-2024): repeated focus on savings rates — FCA publicly challenged banks paying insufficient easy-access savings rates despite base rate rises; resulted in industry-wide rate increases and reputational risk for non-movers
FCA Consumer Duty supervisory programme: first thematic review findings expected 2024-2025; areas under scrutiny include mortgage reversion rates, overdraft harm, savings loyalty penalties
FCA Financial Lives Survey 2022: 27.7% of UK adults have low financial resilience; FCA treating this as systemic vulnerability risk; banks must demonstrate Consumer Duty outcomes for this population
FCA APPF/APP fraud: Financial Ombudsman uphold rate on fraud complaints rising; FCA and PSR jointly pushing for mandatory reimbursement (now in force October 2024)
FCA Mortgage Market Study follow-up: monitoring whether rate switching tools and affordability reforms are working; reversion rate disparity still in regulator sights
PRA stress-testing focus on consumer credit: rising interest rates → arrears risk; PRA expects banks to have modelled credit loss under stress scenarios for personal loans and credit cards

platform_options: Core banking — Thought Machine Vault (cloud-native, used by Lloyds, Atom, Monzo US): API-first, smart contracts for products; high implementation cost but modern architecture
Core banking — Mambu (SaaS cloud core): composable banking, rapid product configuration; used by N26, ABN AMRO, Santander UK (some products); strong for loans and deposits
Core banking — 10x Banking (UK-built, used by Westpac AU, JP Morgan Chase UK): designed for incumbent transformation; native cloud but transformation-path focused
Core banking — Temenos Transact: incumbent legacy modernisation path; large global install base but heavyweight implementation
Savings-as-a-Service — Flagstone, Raisin UK platform: deposit marketplace model; allows banks to place or source deposits without building savings product infrastructure
Lending-as-a-Service — LendInvest (mortgage tech), Nivo (mortgage origination), Eligible (credit risk API): modular lending capability available as API
Credit decisioning — Experian PowerCurve, FICO Blaze, Provenir: hosted credit decisioning and strategy management platforms; avoid building rules engine in-house
KYC/AML — Onfido (ID verification), ComplyAdvantage (sanctions/PEP), Jumio: specialist AML utilities; avoid building name-matching and ID verification infrastructure
Card processing — Marqeta, Thredd (GPS): card issuer processing-as-a-service; modern BIN sponsorship + issuer processing stack for debit and credit cards
Open Banking API — Konsentus, Token.io, Yapily: third-party open banking API connectivity and consent management; avoids building TPP-facing infrastructure from scratch
Insurance distribution — Bain & Company / SCOR insurtech, Open Insurance platforms: white-labelled insurance product distribution; avoids underwriting risk on balance sheet
must_build_in_house: Current account ledger and real-time balance management: the core banking record — must be in-house for regulatory reporting (PRA, FSCS), audit, and control. Core banking platform (Thought Machine/Mambu) may be bought but the bank is the regulated entity and must own the ledger.

Customer relationship data and consent management: primary customer record, marketing preferences, vulnerability flags, Consumer Duty evidence trail — must be sovereign for FCA supervision and GDPR/UK GDPR compliance
Overdraft credit risk decisioning logic: bank-specific credit appetite, pricing strategy, and FCA CONC compliance — the strategy layer must be in-house even if the scoring platform is bought
Fraud detection rules and thresholds: bank must own fraud strategy to meet PSR APP fraud liability requirements and FCA expectations; vendor models are inputs, not the decision
Regulatory reporting pipelines: FSCS eligibility, PRA statistical returns, FCA GABRIEL submissions — must be derived from in-house systems of record
Consumer Duty evidence and outcomes monitoring: FCA requires the firm to produce and retain evidence of consumer outcomes — this is a first-party capability, cannot be delegated to a vendor
buy_candidates: KYC and identity verification: specialist providers (Onfido, Jumio, ComplyAdvantage) deliver better accuracy and faster regulatory updates than in-house builds; commodity capability
Card issuer processing: outsource to Marqeta or Thredd unless card volume justifies in-house processing; scheme rules compliance and fraud tooling better handled by specialist
Credit bureau data and scoring: Experian, Equifax, TransUnion — always buy; running a credit bureau is not a bank activity
Open Banking infrastructure: Yapily / Token.io for TPP-facing APIs if not already built to CMA9 standard; accelerates PSD2 compliance and Open Finance readiness
Savings marketplace connectivity: Raisin or Flagstone API integration to offer best-buy savings rates sourced from partner banks — buy distribution not manufacturing
Insurance distribution platform: white-label or panel insurance for home, travel, life — bank adds distribution value, not underwriting risk
AML transaction monitoring: NICE Actimize, Featurespace ARIC — specialist AI platforms outperform in-house rule sets; buy the engine, own the thresholds
Communications / notifications infrastructure: Twilio, AWS Pinpoint — commodity; do not build SMS/push notification plumbing

primary_revenue_streams: Net interest margin (NIM) on deposits: the spread between rate paid on deposits and rate earned on assets (loans, mortgages, gilts); primary revenue driver; compressed in low-rate environment, expanded in high-rate environment (2022-2024)

Overdraft interest: post-FCA reform, single APR (typically 35-40% EAR) on authorised overdraft balances; reduced from peak revenue but still meaningful for mass-market; persistently high-revenue on 15-20% of current account customers
Personal loan interest margin: spread between cost of funding and interest charged; competitive market (Zopa, Monzo now competing directly); margin around 4-8% NIM on unsecured personal loans
Interchange fees: Mastercard/Visa interchange on debit card transactions (capped at 0.2% under IFR); low per-transaction but high volume; premium accounts may earn higher interchange on credit cards

Premium current account subscription fees: monthly fees (£5-£30/month) for packaged accounts with insurance, travel, and lifestyle benefits; recurring revenue; Lloyds, Barclays, NatWest all operate tiered premium models

Mortgage margin: spread on residential mortgage book (variable-rate reversionary margin is the historical prize; fixed-rate now dominant — margin captured at origination and in the spread to swap rates)
Insurance commission: distribution commission from underwriters for home, life, travel, payment protection products sold through banking relationship; typically 10-25% of premium
Cross-sell and product revenue: credit card annual fee, balance transfer fee; foreign exchange margin on non-Wise/Revolut customers; CHAPS payment fees; safe custody and specialist services
margin_pressure: Neobank no-fee model: Monzo, Starling, Chase UK offer free current accounts with equivalent or better features, creating downward pressure on premium account pricing
FCA overdraft reform (2020): single APR killed unarranged overdraft fees; estimated £200m+ annual industry revenue reduction
Savings rate scrutiny: FCA public pressure on savings rates (2023) forced incumbents to raise easy-access rates; reduced NIM advantage on deposit funding
BNPL market growth: Klarna, Clearpay redirecting credit spend away from credit cards and overdrafts; merchant integration reduces bank's role in the purchase journey
Mortgage price competition: digital lenders (Atom, Molo) and broker platforms (Habito) applying pressure to origination margin; product transfer rates also under scrutiny (FCA MCD review)
Open Banking data portability: price comparison now real-time and automated; customers can identify better savings rates instantly; accelerates rate sensitivity
APP fraud mandatory reimbursement (October 2024): PSR mandatory reimbursement up to £85,000 creates direct P&L exposure; cost of fraud losses moves from customer to bank
Basel 3.1 / CRD VI (implementation 2025-2026): higher capital requirements under standardised approach for retail exposures; increases cost of unsecured lending
cross_sell_hooks: Current account to mortgage: salary credit data as income verification signal; primary account as proof of relationship for mortgage origination — critical retention lever
Current account to personal loan: spending pattern and balance data for pre-approved lending offers; overdraft-to-loan conversion is a high-margin switch
Current account to savings ISA: tax year triggers for ISA conversion; savings pots as gateway to structured savings products
Mortgage to home insurance: completion event as natural trigger for buildings and contents insurance cross-sell; bancassurance margin
Current account to investment: salary credit + savings balance as trigger for investment platform or cash ISA upsell; Nutmeg (Chase UK) model shows integration value
Overdraft to debt consolidation loan: Consumer Duty requires fair value assessment but debt consolidation at lower APR is genuinely beneficial and high margin
Savings to fixed-term deposits: rate rise environment creates opportunity to move easy-access balances to fixed-term products with higher NIM

sub_capabilities.name: Current Accounts
sub_capabilities.description: Provision, operation, and lifecycle management of personal current accounts including debit cards, Faster Payments, CHAPS, Direct Debits, standing orders, CASS participation, and overdraft credit facilities. The primary customer relationship anchor for the retail banking capability.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Current accounts share the same retail customer base and regulatory framework (BCOBS, Consumer Duty) as savings products — they are different product features of a single customer relationship, not a separate market. No specialist entrant has separated current account infrastructure from savings infrastructure at the platform level; even Monzo and Starling operate a unified customer ledger. Overdraft as a credit product sits within CONC but shares the customer's current account record and balance. CASS data confirms customers view their current account as the primary relationship anchor from which other products flow — it is the core of the capability, not a separable unit.

sub_capabilities.name: Savings & Deposits
sub_capabilities.description: Origination and management of personal savings products: instant-access savings accounts, cash ISAs, fixed-term deposits, and notice accounts. Includes interest calculation, FSCS eligibility determination, and ISA manager obligations under HMRC.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Although savings are being unbundled by Chip, Plum, and Raisin (deposit marketplace), these platforms do not represent a fundamentally different regulatory framework — they are still subject to BCOBS and FSCS rules and many use bank balance sheets underneath. Within an incumbent bank, savings share the customer identity, KYC record, Consumer Duty evidence trail, and FSCS reporting infrastructure with the current account. ISA manager obligations (HMRC reporting) sit alongside, not separate from, the banking licence. The shared lifecycle (savings opened from current account, funded by salary credit, managed via the same app) means retention within the parent capability results in less duplication and simpler data ownership. Note: the competitive threat from savings fintechs is captured in design decisions — the bank must invest in rate competitiveness and feature parity, but this is a product strategy decision, not an architectural one.

sub_capabilities.name: Personal Lending
sub_capabilities.description: Origination and servicing of unsecured personal credit products: personal loans (fixed-term, fixed-rate), overdrafts (authorised facilities on current accounts), and overdraft management including persistent debt identification and remediation under FCA CONC rules.

promotion_test.market_evidence: Personal lending in UK retail banking shares the same customer population, KYC/AML infrastructure, and credit bureau integration as current accounts and savings. While CONC governs credit products separately from BCOBS, both fall within the FCA retail conduct regime and Consumer Duty applies to both. Overdrafts are mechanically inseparable from the current account — the balance is on the same ledger. Personal loans originate from the same customer relationship and credit history signals. Key market evidence: even Zopa Bank and Monzo (which do operate as credit-specialist challengers) built current account infrastructure first — the data from the transactional relationship is the input to personal lending decisioning. The shared customer base and credit data lifecycle (salary credit → creditworthiness signal → pre-approved loan offer) is the core integration point that argues for retention. Distinct scalability is not demonstrated — personal loan volume correlates with current account customer growth.

sub_capabilities.name: Mortgages
sub_capabilities.description: Origination, underwriting, and servicing of residential mortgages (owner-occupied and buy-to-let) including rate selection, AIP/full application processing, valuation coordination, legal completion, and ongoing account management through the mortgage lifecycle.

promotion_test.market_evidence: All four promotion criteria are met: (1) Distinct participants — the mortgage origination process involves specialist third parties absent from current account or personal lending journeys: RICS-accredited surveyors/valuers, conveyancing solicitors (buyer and seller side), HM Land Registry for title transfer, mortgage brokers (regulated under FCA AR/DA regime), and Mortgage Credit Directive intermediaries. The broker channel accounts for 70%+ of UK mortgage originations (UK Finance 2023), confirming the intermediary network as a structurally distinct participant layer. Specialist digital mortgage lenders including Habito (FCA authorised lender), Molo Finance, and Atom Bank operate entirely independently of any current account relationship, confirming that the participant network is viable as a standalone market. (2) Separate regulatory framework — MCOB (Mortgages and Home Finance: Conduct of Business sourcebook) is a dedicated FCA sourcebook distinct from BCOBS (current accounts) and CONC (consumer credit). MCOB governs KFI/ESIS disclosure, affordability assessment (Mortgage Market Review 2014), responsible lending rules, arrears and forbearance (MCOB 13), and switching/porting rules. The MCD (Mortgage Credit Directive, transposed 2016) adds cross-border mortgage rules. These regulatory obligations do not overlap with retail deposit or personal lending obligations. (3) Distinct lifecycle — the mortgage lifecycle spans decades: application → AIP → full offer → exchange → completion → rate review/product transfer → redemption. The valuation, legal, and Land Registry phases have no equivalent in current account or personal lending journeys. The mortgage origination SLA (days to offer, days to completion) is driven by the housing market, surveyor availability, and conveyancing pipeline — entirely independent of retail deposit transaction volumes. (4) Independent scalability — mortgage volumes are driven by housing market cycles (house price growth, interest rate expectations, Help to Buy schemes, Stamp Duty holidays) that are entirely independent of current account or savings product growth. During 2020-2021 Stamp Duty holiday, UK mortgage approvals hit 10-year highs while retail deposit growth was driven by pandemic saving — inversely correlated. Specialist mortgage lenders (Nationwide, TSB mortgage-only proposition, Molo, Atom) scale their mortgage operations independently of any retail transaction banking infrastructure.

sub_capabilities.name: Credit Cards
sub_capabilities.description: Origination, management, and servicing of personal credit cards including credit limit management, minimum payment and full settlement, balance transfers, purchases, cash advances, Section 75 liability, and rewards/cashback programmes.

promotion_test.market_evidence: All four promotion criteria are met: (1) Distinct participants — credit card operations require a network of participants absent from retail deposit or personal lending journeys: Mastercard or Visa card schemes (network rules, interchange, chargebacks), acquiring banks (for merchant-side transaction processing), merchants (chargeback and dispute resolution), card processing platforms (Marqeta, Thredd/GPS, FIS, TSYS), and in the case of co-brand/affinity cards, the brand partner (airline, retailer). Specialist pure-play UK credit card issuers (New Day — Aqua, Marbles, Opus; Capital One UK; Vanquis Bank) operate entirely independently of any current account relationship and have large market share in the near-prime segment, confirming that credit card issuance is a viable standalone market with its own participant ecosystem. (2) Separate regulatory framework — credit cards are governed by CONC (Consumer Credit sourcebook) under the Consumer Credit Act 1974 including Section 75 joint and several liability, regulated credit agreement disclosure requirements, minimum repayment rules (FCA PS19/4 raised minimum payments to reduce persistent debt), and the PCI-DSS security standard mandated by card schemes. Card scheme membership rules (Visa/Mastercard Operating Regulations) impose contractual obligations on issuers that are entirely separate from banking conduct rules. PCI-DSS compliance, including cardholder data environment (CDE) segregation, creates distinct technical and audit obligations. (3) Distinct lifecycle — the credit card lifecycle (application → credit assessment → card issuance/personalisation → activation → transaction monitoring → statement cycle → minimum payment collection → limit review → balance transfer → dispute resolution → default/collections → account closure/write-off) does not map onto the current account or personal loan lifecycle. Statement cycles, interest-free periods, and minimum payment cascades are specific product mechanics with no equivalent in other retail products. The dispute and chargeback lifecycle (VISA/MC dispute rules, FOS escalation) is a parallel process unique to card networks. (4) Independent scalability — credit card spend volumes are driven by consumer confidence, retail sales, and travel (the latter correlated with but not identical to GDP), with strong seasonal patterns (Christmas, Black Friday) that differ from salary and savings cycles. Interchange revenue scales with card-present and card-not-present transaction volumes independently of deposit balances. Premium rewards programmes scale with high-spending customers who may hold deposits elsewhere. Capital One UK, New Day, and Vanquis all demonstrate that credit card books can grow independently of any deposit-taking infrastructure.

sub_capabilities.name: Insurance Distribution
sub_capabilities.description: Distribution of retail insurance products through the banking relationship: home insurance (buildings and contents), travel insurance, life insurance (term and whole-of-life), payment protection insurance replacement products, and packaged account insurance. The bank acts as an insurance intermediary (not underwriter) subject to IDD and ICOBS.

promotion_test.market_evidence: All four promotion criteria are met: (1) Distinct participants — insurance distribution inherently involves participants outside the banking value chain: insurance underwriters (Aviva, AXA, Legal & General, Lloyd's syndicates), reinsurers, actuaries, loss adjusters, claims handlers, and the FCA as insurance conduct regulator (separate ICOBS supervision from BCOBS). The Insurance Distribution Directive (IDD) created a distinct intermediary category for banks distributing insurance (appointed representatives, tied agents, or MGA structures). Direct-line insurers (Direct Line Group, Admiral, LV=) and insurtech disruptors (Bought By Many, Lemonade UK) operate entirely without a banking relationship, confirming that insurance distribution is a viable standalone market. The bancassurance model (Lloyds + Scottish Widows, Barclays + Aviva, NatWest + Aviva partnership) treats insurance as a separately managed distribution relationship, not an embedded function. (2) Separate regulatory framework — ICOBS (Insurance: Conduct of Business sourcebook) is a distinct FCA sourcebook from BCOBS and CONC. The Insurance Distribution Directive (IDD, transposed 2018) imposes separate training requirements (15 hours CPD per year for insurance distributors), product governance obligations under PROD (separate from banking PROD requirements), and demands for information at the point of sale distinct from banking disclosure. Insurance products are also regulated by the Prudential Regulation Authority on the underwriting side. FCA PROD 4 (insurance product oversight and governance) is a standalone obligation. PPI remediation history (FCA PS17/3, £38bn in redress) illustrates that insurance mis-selling creates a distinct liability profile from banking conduct breaches. (3) Distinct lifecycle — insurance products have a product lifecycle (quote → underwrite → bind → policy issuance → premium collection → mid-term adjustment → claim → renewal → lapse/cancellation) that does not map onto any banking product lifecycle. Claims handling, which may involve loss adjusters and third-party administrators, has no banking equivalent. Annual renewal cycles create a distinct retention and repricing dynamic. Bancassurance relationships are managed through separate policy administration systems (Applied Epic, Guidewire, Majesco) that are entirely independent of core banking systems. (4) Independent scalability — insurance demand is driven by life events (home purchase, travel, family formation) and regulatory triggers (buildings insurance required for mortgage completion) that are partially correlated with but structurally independent of banking transaction volumes. The packaged account insurance model (fixed monthly fee covering travel/breakdown/gadget) scales with premium account subscriber count, but the underlying insurance capacity, actuarial reserving, and claims operations scale against risk pools driven by weather events, travel volumes, and healthcare costs — entirely independent of deposit or lending dynamics. Specialist bank-independent insurance distributors (GoCompare, MoneySuperMarket, Confused.com) handle higher volumes than any bancassurance operation, confirming independent scalability.

design_decisions.decision: Retain Current Accounts, Savings & Deposits, and Personal Lending as a single deployable capability (CAP-001) rather than splitting into three separate capabilities
design_decisions.rationale: These three sub-capabilities share a single customer identity, a single KYC/AML record, a unified credit bureau integration point, and a common Consumer Duty evidence trail. The bank's competitive advantage in retail banking lies in data from the transactional relationship (salary credits, spending patterns, savings behaviour) informing lending decisioning — splitting these into separate deployment boundaries would require synchronous cross-capability calls on the critical path of overdraft decisioning and loan pre-approval, creating latency risk and eventual consistency problems on financial balances. From a regulatory perspective, FSCS eligibility determination requires a unified view of both deposit and credit balances (net eligible deposits). The market evidence (even neobanks like Monzo and Starling maintain a unified retail ledger rather than separating current account and savings infrastructure) supports this architectural choice.
alternatives_considered: Split Current Accounts, Savings, and Personal Lending into three separate capabilities each with their own database and deployment unit
Separate Personal Lending as its own capability given CONC as distinct regulatory framework
design_decisions.rejected_because: Splitting would require cross-capability consistency guarantees on financial balances — the overdraft facility is on the same ledger as the current account balance, and these cannot be eventually consistent. Separate CONC governance for personal lending is handled within the capability through dedicated governance rules and Consumer Duty outcomes monitoring, without requiring a separate deployment boundary. The overhead of three separate services, API contracts, and deployment pipelines is not justified by the sub-capability promotion test (none of the three retained sub-capabilities meet 3+ criteria).

design_decisions.decision: Promote Mortgages (CAP-001.04) to a standalone capability
design_decisions.rationale: The mortgage origination journey involves a structurally distinct participant network (surveyors, conveyancers, HM Land Registry, mortgage brokers), a dedicated regulatory framework (MCOB, MCD, MRR), a decades-long lifecycle that bears no resemblance to the retail deposit lifecycle, and demand drivers (housing market cycles, Bank Rate expectations, Stamp Duty policy) that are entirely independent of retail banking transaction volumes. The 70%+ broker-originated market share in UK mortgages confirms that the intermediary channel is the dominant distribution mechanism — embedding mortgage origination within the retail banking capability would create a complex multi-participant orchestration problem inside a deployment unit whose primary audience is direct retail customers. Specialist mortgage lenders (Habito, Molo, Atom) demonstrate that the capability is independently viable.
alternatives_considered: Retain mortgages within retail banking as a sub-capability, arguing that the primary customer relationship is in the current account
Create a mortgage sub-capability within retail banking but with a dedicated service boundary
design_decisions.rejected_because: The broker channel, MCOB regulatory obligations (separate compliance monitoring), and housing market scaling requirements create a deployment unit that would be qualitatively different from the retail deposit and lending platform. Shared deployment would couple the release cycle of the mortgage origination system (complex multi-party workflow, HM Land Registry integrations) to the current account platform (high-frequency transaction processing), which is an inappropriate coupling. Retaining it as a retained sub-capability with a dedicated service boundary would achieve only partial separation — the promotion test result (4/4 criteria met) clearly indicates full promotion.

design_decisions.decision: Promote Credit Cards (CAP-001.05) to a standalone capability
design_decisions.rationale: Credit card issuance requires card scheme membership (Visa/Mastercard Operating Regulations), PCI-DSS compliance with cardholder data environment (CDE) segregation, interchange settlement with the card networks, and a statement/minimum payment cycle that is architecturally distinct from the current account transaction model. The dispute and chargeback lifecycle governed by scheme rules has no equivalent in retail banking. The near-prime credit card market (New Day, Vanquis, Capital One UK) operates entirely independently of any banking relationship, demonstrating that the capability is viable as a standalone unit. PCI-DSS CDE requirements effectively mandate infrastructure segregation for cardholder data, which aligns directly with capability promotion to a separate deployment boundary.
alternatives_considered: Retain credit cards within personal lending as both are consumer credit products under CONC
Retain credit cards within retail banking given the cross-sell relationship from current account
design_decisions.rejected_because: PCI-DSS CDE segregation requirements create a practical mandate for infrastructure separation regardless of the promotion test outcome. The card network participant layer (Visa/Mastercard scheme rules, acquiring banks, merchants, chargeback processors) is entirely absent from the personal lending or current account value chain. Conflating credit card servicing with personal lending would merge two systems with fundamentally different statement cycles, payment waterfall logic (interest-free periods, minimum payment cascades), and fraud management paradigms (CNP fraud vs application fraud). The financial risk from Section 75 joint liability is a legally distinct obligation from CONC personal loan defaults.

design_decisions.decision: Promote Insurance Distribution (CAP-001.06) to a standalone capability
design_decisions.rationale: Insurance distribution within a bank is structurally a brokerage/intermediary function governed by ICOBS and IDD, not a banking function. The underwriter relationship, actuarial data flows, claims handling, and annual renewal lifecycle require integration with insurance-specific systems (policy administration, claims management) that are architecturally incompatible with the retail banking platform. PPI mis-selling history (£38bn in redress, FCA PS17/3) demonstrates that insurance distribution creates a distinct conduct and liability profile that is better governed, tested, and audited as a separate capability. The bancassurance market structure (Lloyds/Scottish Widows, NatWest/Aviva, Barclays/Aviva as arm's-length partnerships) reflects the industry's own view that insurance is a distribution relationship, not an embedded banking function.
alternatives_considered: Retain insurance distribution as a sub-capability within retail banking, treating it as a product attached to the current account
Model insurance as a cross-cutting technical service rather than a capability
design_decisions.rejected_because: Treating insurance as a sub-capability within retail banking would embed ICOBS compliance obligations, underwriter API integrations, and claims data flows inside the current account deployment unit. The IDD training and competency requirements apply to specific roles (insurance distributors) who are distinct from retail banking staff — this organisational distinction reflects a real functional separation that the capability model should mirror. Modelling it as a technical service is incorrect: a technical service supports capabilities; insurance distribution is itself a capability (an area of institutional responsibility under FCA authorisation as an insurance intermediary).

design_decisions.decision: Scope retail banking capability to consumer (personal) customers only — exclude SME, business, and private banking
design_decisions.rationale: While CMA9 banks often combine personal and business current accounts under a single banking licence, the SME and business banking customer segment involves distinct KYC obligations (Company House verification, beneficial ownership under MLR 2017), distinct credit assessment (business financial statements, cash flow lending), and distinct regulatory considerations (business banking is largely outside Consumer Duty scope). Private banking involves a materially different service model (relationship manager, bespoke pricing, wealth management overlay). Combining these in a single capability artefact would produce an artefact that is too large to serve as a coherent deployment boundary. The journey inventory for each segment is disjoint enough to warrant separate capabilities.
alternatives_considered: Include SME banking as a sub-capability within retail banking
Include a mass-affluent / private banking sub-capability within retail banking
design_decisions.rejected_because: SME banking has distinct participant types (HMRC, Companies House, trade finance counterparties), distinct regulatory obligations (MLR 2017 beneficial ownership, distinct FCA BCOBS applicability thresholds), and a distinct lifecycle (business formation → trading → growth → refinancing → wind-down) that meets the promotion threshold independently. Private banking meets all four promotion criteria due to distinct participants (wealth managers, discretionary fund managers), separate MiFID II suitability obligations, distinct lifecycle, and independent AuM-driven scaling. Both should be separate capability artefacts.

design_decisions.decision: Target core banking platform evaluation (Thought Machine, Mambu, 10x) rather than building a proprietary ledger from scratch
design_decisions.rationale: Modern cloud-native core banking platforms now offer the flexibility, regulatory compliance tooling, and UK market references (Thought Machine: Lloyds, Monzo US; Mambu: Santander UK products; 10x: Chase UK) that make a buy-not-build decision rational for the core ledger. Building a proprietary real-time ledger and product factory is an 18-24 month effort with significant technical risk and ongoing maintenance burden. The bank's competitive advantage lies in customer data, distribution, and relationship management — not in ledger engineering. However, the bank must retain the data model, regulatory reporting derivations, and Customer Duty evidence trail as in-house capabilities layered over any bought core.
alternatives_considered: Build a proprietary real-time ledger and product configuration layer
Extend an existing legacy core banking system with a digital layer
Use a BaaS provider (e.g. Railsr, Solaris) for the full current account infrastructure
design_decisions.rejected_because: Proprietary ledger build: 18-24 month critical path with high execution risk; no competitive advantage in the ledger itself. Legacy extension: technical debt compounds; modern open banking and Consumer Duty obligations require API-first architecture that legacy systems cannot deliver without significant overlay investment. Full BaaS: cedes control of the regulatory relationship — the bank is the authorised firm and cannot delegate its PRA/FCA obligations to a BaaS provider; also creates concentration risk if the BaaS provider fails.

design_decisions.decision: Treat BNPL as a personal lending product variant rather than a distinct sub-capability, pending FCA BNPL regulation
design_decisions.rationale: BNPL regulation (expected FCA 2025-2026) will bring BNPL within the Consumer Credit Act and CONC. When regulated, BNPL will share the same creditworthiness assessment, affordability, and persistent debt obligations as personal loans. Pre-regulation, offering BNPL through the banking channel is a product decision within personal lending, not a new capability. Post-regulation, the bank's BNPL offering will leverage the same credit decisioning, collections, and Consumer Duty infrastructure already built for personal loans. The regulatory convergence argument supports retention within CAP-001.03 (Personal Lending) rather than creating a separate sub-capability.
alternatives_considered: Create a standalone BNPL sub-capability or promote it to a distinct capability
Partner with a BNPL provider (Klarna, Clearpay) rather than offering own product
design_decisions.rejected_because: A standalone BNPL sub-capability before FCA regulation would create architectural divergence that must be unwound once BNPL is brought within CONC — creating rework. The partner model is a valid strategic alternative (captured in build_vs_buy) but is a product strategy decision for the Domain Analyst, not an architectural constraint that drives a distinct capability boundary.
